description: Also called Floyd's Tortoise and Hare, this pattern runs two pointers at different speeds through a linked structure or an implicit sequence to detect cycles, locate midpoints, find the Nth node from the end, and identify cycle entry points — all in O(1) extra space where the naive solution needs a HashSet or an array copy.
important_details: Applies to linked lists, arrays interpreted as a next-pointer function (index hopping), and any deterministic state machine (functional graph).
If a cycle exists, the fast pointer eventually laps the slow pointer and they meet inside the cycle; if fast reaches null, there is no cycle.
Finding the cycle's start needs a second phase: reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time.
A fixed GAP between pointers (rather than a speed difference) solves Nth-from-end problems in a single pass.
The mathematical core: after meeting inside a cycle, the distance from head to cycle-start equals the distance from meeting-point to cycle-start going forward around the loop.
other_relevant_details: The O(1) space guarantee is the whole point — a HashSet of visited nodes solves most of these problems in O(n) space and is the answer an interviewer will ask you to improve on. Many Medium and Hard linked-list problems are a composition of two of these variations (e.g. Reorder List = find middle + reverse second half + merge alternately).

variations.description: Determine whether a structure contains a cycle by checking whether a 2x-speed pointer ever meets a 1x-speed pointer.
important_details: Guard both fast != null and fast.next != null before advancing two steps, or you get a NullPointerException on even-length acyclic lists.
The pointers are guaranteed to meet within one full traversal of the cycle if one exists — no iteration bound is needed.
Why speed 2 works: the gap between fast and slow shrinks by exactly 1 per step once both are inside the cycle, so a meeting is inevitable.
Beats the HashSet-of-visited-nodes approach on space (O(1) vs O(n)) with identical O(n) time.

variations.description: After detecting a meeting point, locate the exact node where the cycle begins by resetting one pointer to the head and advancing both at equal speed until they meet again.
important_details: Phase 1 finds any meeting point inside the cycle; phase 2 converts that into the cycle's entry node.

Proof sketch: let a = distance head-to-entry, b = entry-to-meeting, c = meeting-to-entry. Then a = c (mod cycle length), so walking a steps from head and c steps from the meeting point lands on the same node.
Both pointers move ONE step at a time in phase 2 — using speed 2 again is a common and silent bug.
The same two-phase structure answers 'find the duplicate number' when an array is reinterpreted as a linked list.

variations.description: Once the pointers meet inside a cycle, measure the cycle's length by keeping one pointer fixed and walking the other around until it returns, counting steps.
important_details: Cycle length is needed for problems asking for the loop's size, or for the maximum cycle length across a functional graph.
In a functional graph (every node has exactly one outgoing edge), each connected component contains exactly one cycle, so you can measure them independently.
Combining length with the entry point gives you the full structure: a 'rho' shape of a tail plus a loop.
For 'longest cycle in a graph' style problems, a visit-timestamp DFS is usually cleaner than Floyd's, but the counting idea is the same.

problems.name: Maximum Employees to Be Invited to a Meeting

variations.description: Locate the midpoint of a linked list in a single pass: when the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer sits at the middle.
important_details: For even-length lists you must decide which middle you want: starting fast at head gives the SECOND middle, starting fast at head.next (or looping while fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null) gives the FIRST middle.
Splitting problems (merge sort on a list, converting to a balanced BST) usually want the first middle so the left half stays non-empty.
Frequently a subroutine, not the whole answer — pair it with reversal for palindrome checks and reordering.
Avoids the two-pass 'count the length, then walk n/2 steps' approach, which is also O(n) but touches the list twice.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) single pass. Space: O(1).

variations.description: Instead of differing speeds, advance one pointer exactly N steps ahead and then move both at the same speed — when the leader hits the end, the follower is exactly N nodes from the end.
important_details: Start both pointers at a dummy node so that removing the head itself needs no special case.
The follower ends up at the node BEFORE the target when you want to delete, so advance the leader N+1 times (or start from dummy) depending on your convention.
This is the one-pass solution to a problem whose naive answer is two passes (count length, then walk length-n).
Validate that N does not exceed the list length if the problem does not guarantee it.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) single pass. Space: O(1).

variations.description: Applies Floyd's algorithm where 'next' is not a pointer but a function of the current value — digit-square sums, array index hopping, or duplicate detection where values are reinterpreted as pointers.
important_details: Model the state transition as if it were a linked list: the 'next' of state x is f(x).
In 'Find the Duplicate Number', index i points to index nums[i]; because some value repeats, two indices point to the same place, creating a cycle whose ENTRY is the duplicate value.
Happy Number works the same way with f(x) = sum of squares of digits; a cycle that does not contain 1 means the number is unhappy.
The hard part is recognizing that an array or number problem is secretly a cycle-detection problem — the code afterward is mechanical.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1) — satisfies constraints that forbid modifying the array, unlike the cyclic-sort solution to the same problem.

variations.description: The most common Medium/Hard linked-list composition: split at the middle with fast/slow, reverse the second half in place, then walk both halves in parallel to compare (palindrome) or interleave (reorder).
important_details: Three distinct sub-routines chained together — practice each independently before combining them.
For palindrome checks, stopping the comparison when the second (reversed) half runs out handles both odd and even lengths cleanly.
Interviewers often ask you to restore the list to its original state afterward; be ready to reverse the second half back.
This composite achieves O(n) time and O(1) space where the naive approach copies values into an ArrayList for O(n) space.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1), versus O(n) for the array-copy approach.
